## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775)Discussion

Ischemic stroke is a devastating vascular disease with significant mortality and morbidity. Despite decades of research, no neuroprotective treatment has proven clinically effective.[63](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R63) Time-of-day has emerged as a significant factor underlying the translational gap in stroke management.[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R2),[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R4) Understanding how these rhythms affect stroke responses and prognosis could provide valuable insights for improving therapy. Here, we demonstrate in mice and humans that stroke severity displays diurnal circadian oscillations and identify neutrophil-mediated NETosis and vascular stalling as key mechanisms driving time-of-day–dependent differences in severity. Therefore, strategies targeting neutrophil heterogeneity, inhibiting NET formation, or promoting NET degradation represent promising therapeutic avenues. Importantly, for any of these treatments to be effective, circadian influence must be considered. Identifying the optimal time-of-day for intervention could maximize their impact on cerebral perfusion in stroke but also in other pathologies where circadian rhythms and inflammation are pivotal.[64](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R64)–[66](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R66)

In this work, we used permanent and transient mouse models to evaluate the influence of circadian rhythms on stroke outcome. Our findings demonstrate that infarct size is significantly larger when stroke occurred at ZT5, during the inactive mouse phase, compared with the active phase, showing clear circadian oscillations in the Cosinor model. This pattern was consistent across models, including aged animals, at both normal and reverse cycles, and correlated with neuromotor deficits, such as reduced contralateral forelimb stride length at ZT5 in the footprint test. Similar data were previously observed in mice and rats.[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R4),[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R6),[67](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R67),[68](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R68) Moreover, diurnal oscillations in stroke severity were also observed in human ischemic stroke, in agreement with our animal data and previous studies showing that patients with nighttime stroke onset, that is, during the human inactive period, showed larger core volumes and faster core growth than those during the human active period.[69](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R69),[70](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R70) Importantly, our findings in both species aligned across markers and activity phases: although mice are nocturnal and humans diurnal, infarct volume and associated markers remained congruent when adjusted for each species active phase. This cross-species consistency underscores the relevance of circadian impact on stroke outcome and the robustness of our results.

Circadian rhythms may shape ischemic stroke progression and outcomes by modulating critical components of the ischemic cascade, notably inflammation and immunity.[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R5) Immune cells operate on a circadian schedule, demonstrating 24-hour rhythmicity in resting and activated states. Among them, neutrophils–the first responders after stroke–display circadian variations in numbers, phenotypes, and activation markers.[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R10),[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R26)–[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R28) These fluctuations made us think that neutrophils may influence stroke outcomes depending on the time of the day. Indeed, neutrophil reduction with an anti-Ly6G antibody abolished circadian-dependent differences in stroke outcome. Of note, not only neutrophil numbers seem to be important: the inhibition of the neutrophil clock by genetic strategies with specific-neutrophil deletion of either BMAL1 or CXCR4 eliminated circadian variation in infarct size, demonstrating that both neutrophil count and phenotype affect stroke severity. This effect was confirmed by adoptive transfer experiments wherein similar numbers of Bmal1-knockout–derived neutrophils in brain promoted higher infarcts than WT cells. Altogether, these data support that both neutrophil number and phenotype, by determining localization and functional state, are key modulators of ischemic brain injury.

With the evidence that both neutrophil counts and phenotype shape infarct size in ischemic stroke, we sought to uncover their exact contributions. We found that the temporal pattern of neutrophil infiltration into the brain and, importantly, their location and morphology inside BVs or into the brain parenchyma were different for stroke occurring at ZT5 versus ZT13. In this sense, our data suggest that detrimental actions of neutrophils at ZT5 (when infarcts are larger) occur mainly within BVs rather than the brain parenchyma. A positive correlation between infarct size and neutrophil count was observed only at ZT5, suggesting a more damaging phenotype at this time.

Tissue viability, in addition to collateral flow, is vulnerable to secondary microcirculatory failure,[39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R39),[71](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R71),[72](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R72) where neutrophils play a key role.[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R19),[73](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R73) At ZT5, elongated intravascular neutrophils and neutrophil-platelet aggregates[45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R45) suggest circadian, neutrophil-dependent flow stalling, consistent with functionally distinct neutrophil subtypes based on shape and motility.[74](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R74) Predominant intravascular retention implies poorer perfusion and greater hypoxia, promoting penumbral recruitment into the infarct core. Conversely, greater parenchymal infiltration at ZT13, with fewer neutrophils in the vascular lumen, is consistent with preserved perfusion and limited infarct growth.

Although neutrophils have traditionally been considered detrimental in ischemic stroke,[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R36)–[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R38),[75](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R75),[76](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R76) depletion or infiltration inhibition studies yield inconsistent results, suggesting a more complex role. Neutrophils exhibit a remarkable plasticity and heterogeneity, with distinct subpopulations contributing differently to physiology and pathology.[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R6),[77](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R77)–[80](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R80) Consistent with previous studies showing neutrophil heterogeneity in blood and brain,[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R21)–[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R24) our results support that, on stroke and depending on the time of the day, brain neutrophils display different phenotypes and functions that could either worsen or improve tissue damage after stroke.

Of note, at ZT13, neutrophil clusters are prominent but nearly absent at ZT5. Notably, BNc4 represents an IFN-induced neutrophil cluster activated by IFN signaling, particularly type I (like IFN-α and IFN-β) and type II IFNs (IFN-γ). These cytokines are key immune regulators in viral, inflammatory, and autoimmune contexts. Specifically, the response to IFN drew our attention due to its implications in NETosis[81](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R81)–[84](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R84)—a process whereby neutrophils release web-like structures of DNA, histones, and proteases known as NETs, driving immunothrombosis, inflammation, and blood-brain barrier disruption[81](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R81),[82](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R82),[85](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R85) and contributing to ischemic stroke pathogenesis of ischemic stroke by stalling of brain capillaries.[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R19),[73](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R73)

IFNs promote NETosis through PAD4, essential for histone citrullination and subsequent NET formation, and modulate neutrophil activation state, facilitating NETosis in response to various stimuli, including viral infections.[52](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R52)–[55](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R55) Surprisingly, the BNc4 neutrophil cluster is upregulated at ZT13, when infarct size is smaller. Given the deleterious role of NETosis demonstrated in the context of ischemic stroke,[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R13),[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R17),[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R18),[85](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R85)–[87](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R87) this led us to hypothesize that neutrophils at ZT5 undergo accelerated NETosis and enhanced response to IFN, making them less detectable 12 hours poststroke due to NETosis-induced destruction. Similar findings were reported in COVID-19–associated pulmonary aspergillosis, where neutrophil reduction was attributed to increased destruction via NETosis.[88](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R88) Supporting this, we found increased NETosis at ZT5 compared with ZT13 in both circulating and brain-resident isolated neutrophils. ELISA confirmed higher plasma elastase levels, a NETosis proxy, at ZT5, and brain immunostaining revealed greater NET burden.

Differences in stroke outcome between ZT5 versus ZT13 may stem from reduced blood flow due to NETosis-induced vascular obstruction at ZT5. Consistently, pharmacological or genetic NET inhibition reduced infarct volume only at ZT5, again underscoring circadian dependency. PAD4−/− mice displayed improved collateral flow at ZT5 versus WT, reinforcing the role of NETs in blood flow disruption and suggesting that NETosis exacerbates microvascular stalling in a time-specific manner. Importantly, similar fluctuations in NETosis markers were observed in humans, correlating with collateral flow and supporting NETs as an immunothrombotic mechanism hindering cerebral perfusion recovery after stroke.

Finally, treatment with DNase-I, which degrades NETs, effectively reduced infarct volume at ZT5, supporting its potential to counteract time-dependent damage exacerbation from NETosis. These findings are confirmed by recent evidence showing that DNAse-I reduces infarct volumes after in situ thromboembolic stroke, a tPA (tissue-type plasminogen activator)-sensitive stroke mouse model, in the inactive but not in the active rodent phase,[89](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775#R89) highlighting the therapeutic relevance of DNase-I and supporting NET targeting to improve outcomes.

Alternative mechanisms could be playing a role. For instance, neutrophils could release vasoactive mediators, causing vasoconstriction at ZT5. However, neither vascular diameter assessment by pan-laminin staining nor the vasoconstriction gene program revealed major differences between ZT5 and ZT13 (data not shown), suggesting overt vasoconstriction was not a predominant feature at the times studied.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822775)Conclusions

Collectively, our findings suggest that circadian regulation of neutrophil count, phenotype, and neutrophil-related functions such as NETosis determines ischemic injury severity. This may explain the translational failures of neuroprotective therapies and suggests that targeting neutrophil function and NET formation and degradation may be more effective at specific times of the day. Our data also support personalized chronotherapy for stroke management based on specific, NETosis-inspired, plasma biomarkers. Future therapies should integrate chronobiological principles to optimize outcomes. It is worth noting that ongoing clinical trials are investigating the efficacy and safety of several therapies, including DNase-I, on various inflammatory and neurovascular pathologies. Our studies will help establish the effects of this and other strategies in a clinical context, refining treatment timing and conditions according to circadian rhythms. Accounting for circadian modulation of neutrophils and their associated processes, such as NETosis, could yield novel, effective strategies for stroke therapy.

  "evidence": "**From 'Diurnal Oscillations in Human Stroke Severity, Immunothrombosis, and NET Markers Linked to Collateral Circulation' (Results):**

Finally, to explore the time-of-day–dependent influence of NETosis on ischemic stroke severity in humans, we next analyzed data from 366 patients with known time of stroke onset (Figure 7). Patients with stroke had a median age of 76 years, 51.2% were female, and they displayed a median National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale score on admission of 10 (Tables S5 through S7). Using an adjusted Cosinor model fitted to the time of admission, we found that different hematologic parameters, including neutrophil and platelet counts, mean platelet volume and plasma markers associated with immunothrombosis (sCD40L [soluble CD40 ligand]) and NET release (elastase and MPO) all displayed diurnal fluctuations, peaking at 9 and 6-7 pm, respectively (Figure 7A; Figures S16 and S17; Table S8). Supporting the notion that NET formation and vascular stalling influence infarct progression and stroke severity, our stroke patient cohort also displayed time-of-day oscillations in several stroke outcome parameters, including admission and 24-hour NIHSS score and infarct volumes, that aligned with the corresponding circadian rhythmicity observed for NET release and immunothrombosis markers (Figure 7B; Table S8).

Finally, given the potential relationship between collateral circulation and stroke severity, we explored whether this association also extended to markers of NETosis in a subcohort of 349 patients with stroke. For that, violin plots were generated to illustrate the distribution of key clinical markers, including first prognostic markers (admission NIHSS score and infarct volume) and markers of NETs formation (admission elastase and MPO) in patients with either good or poor collateral circulation (Figure 7C). As expected, patients with stroke with good collateral circulation showed lower infarct volume and admission NIHSS score than those with a poor collateral circulation (Figure 7C) and, importantly and supporting our previous results, plasma levels of admission elastase were also increased in patients with a poor collateral flow strongly supporting that NETosis is also a key factor in the differential susceptibility of humans to stroke, depending on circadian rhythms.

**From 'Inhibition of NET Formation Abolishes Circadian Differences in Stroke Outcome' (Results):**

To investigate the influence of NETosis on infarct volume after ischemic stroke, we next inhibited NET formation by 2 distinct strategies: a pharmacological approach and a genetic intervention, both of which target the PAD4 (peptidyl arginine deiminase 4), a key enzyme for histone citrullination during NET formation (Figure 6). We first administered chloramidine, a pharmacological inhibitor of PAD4, and measured infarct volumes 24 hours postsurgery (Figure 6A). NET inhibition by chloramidine produced a significant reduction in the lesion size compared with the vehicle-treated group at ZT5, but not at ZT13 (Figure 6B). Similarly, PAD4−/− mice showed a significant reduction in the infarct volume at ZT5 compared with control mice but not at ZT13 (Figure 6C), supporting the time-restricted contribution of NETs in the brain damage during the inactive phase (ZT5).

The role of NETs during ischemic stroke was also confirmed in another experimental stroke model induced by in situ thrombin injection (Figure S14). In addition, NET inhibition improved the CBF recovery after MCA occlusion, consistent with reduced vascular stalling (Figure 6D through 6K; Figure S15). Quantification of blood flow in this region in control and PAD4−/− mice subjected to surgery at ZT5 demonstrated higher recovery of blood flow in the ipsilesional cortical area in PAD4−/− mice (Figure 6D through 6G). In agreement with a recovered CBF, vascular occluded segments in this cortical region by both neutrophils and platelets were also reduced in PAD4−/− mice (Figure 6H through 6K). Finally, the intravenous administration of DNase-I after MCA occlusion, as a strategy for reducing NET-dependent stalling at ZT5, caused a marked reduction in infarct volume at this time (Figure 6L).

Because neutrophils are the first immune cells responding and mediating damage early after stroke onset, we tested the possibility that the circadian control of neutrophil activation was an underlying mechanism controlling the variations in stroke damage. For that, we first depleted neutrophils by treating mice with an anti-Ly6G–specific antibody and evaluated the infarct size 48 hours after stroke in mice subjected to surgery at ZT5 and ZT13 (Figure 2A). … Importantly, antibody-mediated neutrophil depletion reduced infarct size at ZT5 compared with the isotype-treated group and led to the loss of the circadian pattern in infarct size (Figure 2C). … Thus, we decided to check whether time-of-day variation in stroke outcome was dependent not only on neutrophil numbers as demonstrated by the depletion model, but also on the circadian phenotype of neutrophils. For that, we performed stroke surgery at ZT5 and ZT13 and evaluated infarct size in mice in which the neutrophil clock was altered by genetic strategies (Figure 2D and 2E). … We generated neutrophil-specific Bmal- and Cxcr4-deficient mice, referred to as Bmal Neu and Cxcr4 Neu… We found that, in both Bmal Neu and Cxcr4 Neu mice, ischemic damage became arrhythmic as circadian differences in infarct size between ZT5 and ZT13 were completely abolished (Figure 2F).

**From 'Circadian Control of Neutrophil Transcription After Stroke' (Results):**

Our findings indicate that neutrophils influenced by circadian rhythms play distinct roles in ischemic stroke outcomes. To check whether circadian rhythms induce distinct neutrophil programs during stroke, we next investigated the transcriptional signature of neutrophils located in the ischemic brain (Figure 4A). We performed scRNA-seq analysis on sorted CD11b+ Ly6G+ neutrophils from the ischemic tissue, 12 hours after stroke in both ZT5 and ZT13 ischemic mice. … We next evaluated the transcriptional profile of brain neutrophils for different core and effector neutrophil functions … and found that each neutrophil subcluster displayed different scores for chemotaxis, activation, ROS production, and even granule biosynthesis. We next checked whether ischemic stroke at different day times modulates the presence of the different neutrophil programs in the brain. As observed in Figure 4F through 4H, the percentage of cells in each cluster dramatically fluctuates with the time of the day, wherein neutrophils allocated in BNc2 and BNc4 belonged mainly to the ZT13 ischemic group (Figure 4F and 4G). … In contrast, cluster BNc1 (and, to a smaller degree, the BNc3) was the most represented one in the ischemic brain when the stroke was induced at midday, with an almost 2-fold increase compared with ZT13 (Figure 4H).

**From 'Circadian Modulation of Neutrophil Function Promotes NET Formation After Stroke' (Results):**

We asked whether the differential capacity to form NETs of neutrophils at ZT5 could explain the differences in the number and subsets of infiltrated neutrophils, CBF recovery, and stroke outcome in a time-of-day–dependent manner. To address this, we compared the ex vivo capacity of neutrophils isolated 12 hours after surgery at ZT5 or at ZT13. We stimulated the neutrophils with the NET-inducing compound phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA) and analyzed NETs by colocalization of extracellular DNA (Sytox), MPO, and cit-H3 (citrullinated histone 3; Figure 5). … We found that neutrophils isolated from the infarcted brain at ZT5 formed more NETs than those at ZT13 (Figure 5B and 5C; Figure S12). … The higher potential of neutrophils from ischemic ZT5 mice to form NETs was also suggested by the presence of NETs in the ischemic brain 12 hours after stroke (Figure 5F and 5G; Figure S14). … Taken together, our findings indicate that NETosis is the circadian-dependent mechanism by which neutrophils drive vascular stalling after stroke.",
  "summary": "The study demonstrates that harmful neutrophil subsets, driven by circadian rhythms, exacerbate ischemic stroke outcomes. In patients, diurnal oscillations of NET-related biomarkers (elastase, MPO, sCD40L) peak during the inactive phase (evening/night) and correlate with poor collateral circulation and larger infarct volumes. In mice, neutrophils during the inactive phase (ZT5) exhibit an activated, NET-prone phenotype, causing microvascular stalling and reduced cerebral blood flow recovery. Inhibiting NET formation pharmacologically (chloramidine, DNase-I) or genetically (PAD4 knockout) abolishes circadian differences in infarct size and improves collateral perfusion, confirming that NETosis is a key mechanism of brain injury. Circadian control of neutrophils is mediated by the intrinsic clock genes Bmal1 and CXCR4, which regulate neutrophil numbers, phenotype, and transcriptional heterogeneity. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed distinct neutrophil clusters (e.g., BNc1 at ZT5, BNc2/BNc4 at ZT13) with differential pro-inflammatory, IFN-response, and NETosis signatures. Together, these findings establish that circadian regulation of neutrophil NETosis drives vascular occlusion and stroke severity, and that targeting NET formation or timing therapy could offer chronotherapeutic opportunities."

Please process the following webpage content and user goal to extract relevant information:

## **Webpage Content** 
Title: Neutrophil extracellular traps regulate ischemic stroke brain injury

URL Source: https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225

Markdown Content:
NETs are present in brain tissue from ischemic stroke patients. To examine whether NETs are present in human brain tissue after ischemic stroke, we obtained brain specimens from 3 patients who died after ischemic stroke. Brain specimens were stained with the neutrophil-specific markers neutrophil elastase (NE) and myeloperoxidase (MPO), as well as with citrullinated histone H3 (H3cit), a marker for neutrophils undergoing NET formation. In agreement with a previous report ([17](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#B17)), neutrophils were readily found in ipsilesional brain tissue from all stroke patients ([Figure 1](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F1) and [Supplemental Figure 1](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#sd); supplemental material available online with this article; [https://doi.org/10.1172/JCI154225DS1](https://doi.org/10.1172/JCI154225DS1)), while neutrophils were mostly absent in contralateral brain tissue from stroke patients ([Supplemental Figure 2](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#sd)). Several neutrophils (NE and MPO double-positive cells) in the ipsilesional brain tissue stained positive for H3cit, indicating they either were in the process of NET formation or had already formed a NET ([Figure 1](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F1) and [Supplemental Figure 1](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#sd)). In all patients, both extracellular NETs (arrows) and neutrophils undergoing NET formation (arrowheads) were found ([Figure 1, A–D](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F1), [Supplemental Figure 1](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#sd), and [Supplemental Video 1](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#sd)). In all cases, NE, MPO, DNA, and citrullinated histones colocalized with each other ([Figure 1](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F1) and [Supplemental Figure 1](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#sd)). Neutrophils in the contralesional hemisphere did not stain for H3cit ([Supplemental Figure 2](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#sd)).

[![Image 1: NETs are found in ipsilesional brain tissue from ischemic stroke patients.](https://dm5migu4zj3pb.cloudfront.net/manuscripts/154000/154225/small/JCI154225.f1.gif)](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225/figure/1)[Figure 1](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225/figure/1)

NETs are found in ipsilesional brain tissue from ischemic stroke patients. Ipsilesional brain tissue was obtained from the NIH NeuroBioBank from 3 patients who died after ischemic stroke. (**A**–**D**) NETs were identified by colocalization of myeloperoxidase (MPO; red), neutrophil elastase (NE; white), citrullinated histone H3 (H3cit; green), and DNA (DAPI; blue). (**A**) Neutrophils were in different stages of NET formation, with nuclear decondensation and intracellular H3cit staining (arrowheads) and released extracellular NETs (arrows) frequently observed. Scale bar: 30 μm. (**B**) Top row: High-power magnification image of an extracellular NET with the separate color channels. Bottom left: _z_ projection illustrates colocalization of different NET markers. Bottom right: 3D rendering shows H3cit+ DNA release from a neutrophil. Scale bar: 5 μm. (**C**) High-power magnification image of 3 neutrophils in different stages of NET formation. Scale bar: 5 μm. (**D**) Example of an intravascular neutrophil-rich thrombus from a separate patient. Scale bars: 30 μm. (**E**) NETs were identified by colocalization of MPO (red), H3cit (green), and DNA (DAPI; blue), and platelets were stained with CD42b (white). Scale bar: 10 μm. Platelets associated with NETs within a vessel in the ipsilesional stroke brain are shown. Images are representative of 2 separate patients (**A**–**C**, patient 1; **D** and **E**, patient 2), representing findings from a total of 3 patients.

In several patients, H3cit+ neutrophils were found in cerebral blood vessels, trapped in neutrophil-rich microthrombi occasionally occluding the vessel lumen ([Figure 1, D and E](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F1), and [Supplemental Figure 1D](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#sd)). To investigate the contribution of platelets to this phenomenon, we stained consecutive brain slides for DNA, MPO, H3cit, and CD42b, a platelet-specific marker. As expected, platelets bridged neutrophils in these microthrombi, implying a role for platelet-neutrophil interactions in mediating microthrombus formation in clinical ischemic stroke ([Figure 1E](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F1)). Interestingly, many of the neutrophils found in contact with platelets were undergoing NET formation, suggesting that platelets participate in NET release. Consistent with these findings, we observed NETs predominantly in platelet-rich areas of stroke thrombi retrieved from patients undergoing thrombectomy ([Supplemental Figure 3](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#sd)). Notably, as in brain tissue, all MPO+ cells also stained for NE in stroke patient thrombi ([Supplemental Figure 4](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#sd)), implying that MPO in thrombi and brain tissue is mainly of neutrophil origin.

Plasma markers of immunothrombosis are increased in ischemic stroke patients, and NET markers correlate with stroke outcomes. To further address immunothrombosis in ischemic stroke, we measured markers of coagulation (D-dimer; [Figure 2A](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F2)), platelet activation (platelet factor 4 [PF4]; [Figure 2B](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F2)), neutrophil activation (calprotectin; [Figure 2C](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F2)), NET formation (H3cit, [Figure 2D](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F2); and MPO-DNA complexes, [Figure 2E](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F2)), and NET degradation potential (DNase activity; [Figure 2F](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F2)) in plasma from matched healthy donors and stroke patients ([Supplemental Table 1](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#sd)). Markers of immunothrombosis were significantly elevated and plasma DNase activity was greatly reduced in ischemic stroke patients compared with healthy donors ([Figure 2](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F2)). We next used a Spearman correlation analysis to investigate whether markers of immunothrombosis correlated with either stroke severity at admission or stroke outcomes at discharge ([Supplemental Table 2](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#sd)). Stroke severity at admission did not correlate with immunothrombosis biomarkers. Interestingly, only markers of NET formation correlated with ischemic stroke outcomes (modified Rankin scale at discharge). Both plasma H3cit and MPO-DNA levels positively correlated with stroke outcomes (_r_ = 0.45, _P =_ 0.024, and _r_ = 0.507, _P =_ 0.01, respectively). Sex, comorbidities, thrombolysis, use of antiplatelet drugs or anticoagulation drugs, or ischemic stroke etiology had no effect on plasma NET levels in our cohort ([Supplemental Figure 5](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#sd)).

[![Image 2: Plasma markers of immunothrombosis are increased in ischemic stroke patient](https://dm5migu4zj3pb.cloudfront.net/manuscripts/154000/154225/small/JCI154225.f2.gif)](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225/figure/2)[Figure 2](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225/figure/2)

Plasma markers of immunothrombosis are increased in ischemic stroke patients. Plasma samples were obtained within 48 hours of hospital admission from stroke patients or age- and sex-matched healthy donors (HD). D-dimer (**A**), PF4 (**B**), neutrophil calprotectin (**C**), H3cit (**D**), MPO-DNA complexes (**E**), and DNase activity (**F**) were measured by ELISA. _n =_ 27 per group. Groups were compared by Mann-Whitney test. **_P <_ 0.01, ***_P <_ 0.001, ****_P <_ 0.0001.

Platelet-neutrophil interactions mediate NET formation through HMGB1. Platelets are known for their role in NET formation ([6](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#B6)), and we observed NETs predominantly in platelet-rich areas of ischemic stroke thrombi as well as in microthrombi in the brain ([Figure 1E](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F1) and [Supplemental Figure 3](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#sd)). Additionally, plasma levels of PF4 correlated with both plasma H3cit and MPO-DNA levels in our cohort (_r_ = 0.376, _P =_ 0.024, and _r_ = 0.556, _P =_ 0.001, respectively), implying a role for platelet activation in stroke-induced NET formation. To examine whether platelets could contribute to neutrophil activation and NET formation, we first examined platelet-neutrophil aggregate levels in ischemic stroke patients. Consistent with previous studies ([18](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#B18)), circulating platelet-neutrophil aggregates were significantly increased in stroke patients ([Figure 3A](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F3) and [Supplemental Figure 6](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#sd)). As platelets interact with neutrophils to induce NET formation through different mechanisms, such as danger-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), including HMGB1 ([19](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#B19), [20](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#B20)), we examined whether platelet and plasma HMGB1 levels increased during ischemic stroke. Platelets from stroke patients had significantly elevated HMGB1 surface expression ([Figure 3, B and C](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F3)) and increased plasma HMGB1 levels ([Figure 3D](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F3)) compared with healthy donors. Furthermore, HMGB1 predominantly localized at the interface of platelets interacting with neutrophils in ischemic stroke thrombi ([Figure 3E](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F3)). We next examined whether plasma HMGB1 correlated with plasma NET markers and observed that HMGB1 significantly correlated with H3cit and MPO-DNA (_r_ = 0.433, _P =_ 0.0019, and _r_ = 0.3889, _P =_ 0.0057, respectively).

[![Image 3: Platelet HMGB1 is increased in ischemic stroke patients and is found at the](https://dm5migu4zj3pb.cloudfront.net/manuscripts/154000/154225/small/JCI154225.f3.gif)](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225/figure/3)[Figure 3](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225/figure/3)

Platelet HMGB1 is increased in ischemic stroke patients and is found at the interface between platelets and neutrophils in ischemic stroke thrombi. (**A**–**C**) Flow cytometry was performed on diluted whole blood (**A**) and washed platelets (**B** and **C**) isolated from ischemic stroke patients and matched healthy donors (HD) to quantify platelet-neutrophil aggregates and platelet HMGB1 expression levels, respectively. _n =_ 11–12 per group. (**D**) Plasma HMGB1 levels were measured by ELISA in ischemic stroke patients and matched healthy donors. _n =_ 27 per group. (**E**) Ischemic stroke patient thrombi were stained for platelets (CD42b, white), HMGB1 (green), neutrophils (MPO, red) and DNA (DAPI, blue). Scale bar: 10 μm. Image is representative of 7 ischemic stroke thrombi. Groups were compared by unpaired _t_ test (**A**–**C**) or Mann-Whitney test (**D**). **_P <_ 0.01, ***_P <_ 0.001, ****_P <_ 0.0001.

Platelets drive HMGB1 release and NET formation, exacerbating stroke outcomes. To examine the role of platelet HMGB1 in vivo, we used a murine transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (tMCAO) model, in which the right MCA is occluded for 1 hour followed by 23 hours of reperfusion. Using this model, we observed a significant increase in circulating levels of HMGB1 and MPO-DNA complexes 6 and 24 hours after stroke in comparison with sham animals ([Figure 4, A and B](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F4)), consistent with our observations in human ischemic stroke patients. In addition, we readily detected NETs in the brain throughout the ischemic hemisphere 6 and 24 hours after stroke onset ([Figure 4, C and D](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F4), and [Supplemental Figure 7](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#sd)), while NETs and neutrophils were not observed in the contralateral hemisphere (data not shown). As in stroke patients, we observed 3 types of neutrophils (Ly6G and MPO double positive): (a) H3cit-negative, non-NETting neutrophils; (b) extracellular NETs; and (c) neutrophils in the early stages of NET formation ([Figure 4C](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F4)). Furthermore, platelet-neutrophil complexes were frequently observed in stroke brain tissue, and platelets colocalized with NETs ([Figure 4D](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F4)). Importantly, staining in brains from mice after tMCAO was similar to that observed in human ischemic stroke patients (compare [Figure 1](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F1) with [Figure 4](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F4)).

[![Image 4: Characterization of NET formation in a mouse model of ischemic stroke.](https://dm5migu4zj3pb.cloudfront.net/manuscripts/154000/154225/small/JCI154225.f4.gif)](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225/figure/4)[Figure 4](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225/figure/4)

Characterization of NET formation in a mouse model of ischemic stroke. Mice were subjected to 1 hour of tMCAO or sham surgery. Plasma was isolated 6 or 24 hours after stroke onset, and brains were collected and processed for histology. (**A**) MPO-DNA complexes were measured using an in-house MPO-DNA ELISA. _n =_ 4 per group. (**B**) Plasma HMGB1 levels were measured by ELISA. _n =_ 4 per group. (**C**) Brain tissue was stained for the presence of NETs by a combination of Ly6G (white), MPO (red), H3cit (green), and DNA (DAPI, blue). Scale bar: 50 μm. (**D**–**F**) Both neutrophils not undergoing NET formation (H3cit–, highlighted in **D**) and neutrophils undergoing NET formation (H3cit+, highlighted in **E** and **F**) were observed. Scale bars: 25 μm. (**G**–**I**) Brain tissue was stained for the colocalization of NETs with platelets by a combination of MPO (red), H3cit (green), platelets (CD41, white), and DNA (DAPI, blue). Scale bars: 15 μm. Images are representative of 4 mice. Groups were compared by ordinary 1-way ANOVA. *_P <_ 0.05, **_P <_ 0.01.

In order to study whether platelet HMGB1 drives NET formation in ischemic stroke, we depleted platelets immediately after stroke onset with an anti-GPIb antibody ([Figure 5, A–D](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F5), and [Supplemental Figure 8A](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#sd)). Twenty-four hours after stroke, thrombocytopenic mice had significantly lower levels of circulating HMGB1 compared with mice treated with an IgG control (5.9 ± 2 ng/mL vs. 9.5 ± 2.8 ng/mL, respectively; [Figure 5A](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F5)). Moreover, the reduction of plasma HMGB1 in thrombocytopenic mice was associated with a significant reduction in plasma MPO-DNA complexes 24 hours after stroke (136% ± 53.1% vs. 295.6% ± 128.1%; [Figure 5B](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F5)). As plasma HMGB1 and NET levels were decreased, we next examined whether thrombocytopenic mice were protected from ischemic stroke brain injury. Consistent with a role for platelet-HMGB1-induced NET formation in ischemic stroke, thrombocytopenic mice were protected from brain injury (45.3 ± 20.3 mm 3 vs. 88.2 ± 35.2 mm 3; [Figure 5, C and D](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F5)) and had improved neurological function ([Supplemental Figure 8](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#sd), B and C). To further establish a causal role for HMGB1 in mediating NET formation after stroke, we treated thrombocytopenic mice with recombinant HMGB1 (rHMGB1). rHMGB1 increased plasma NET levels in platelet-depleted mice (245.1% ± 81.1% vs. 123.1% ± 35.6%; [Figure 5E](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F5)) and exacerbated ischemic stroke brain injury (56.4 ± 19.3 mm 3 vs. 28.4 ± 11.2 mm 3; [Figure 5, F and G](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F5), and [Supplemental Figure 9](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#sd), A and B).

[![Image 5: Platelets mediate HMGB1 release, contributing to detrimental NET formation](https://dm5migu4zj3pb.cloudfront.net/manuscripts/154000/154225/small/JCI154225.f5.gif)](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225/figure/5)[Figure 5](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225/figure/5)

Platelets mediate HMGB1 release, contributing to detrimental NET formation in a mouse model of ischemic stroke. Mice were subjected to 1 hour of tMCAO followed by 23 hours of reperfusion or sham surgery. Plasma was isolated and brains were analyzed for ischemic stroke brain damage by TTC staining 24 hours after stroke onset. Upon TTC staining, live brain tissue will stain red, while dead brain tissue will remain white (outlined with black dotted line). (**A**–**D**) Immediately after stroke onset, mice were injected with a platelet-depleting antibody or IgG control. Twenty-four hours later, plasma HMGB1 (**A**) and MPO-DNA complexes (**B**) were assessed as well as brain infarct volume (**C** and **D**). _n =_ 6 for sham mice; _n =_ 9 for groups subjected to stroke. (**E**–**G**) Immediately after stroke onset, mice were injected with a platelet-depleting antibody. One hour later, either recombinant HMGB1 (rHMGB1) or vehicle was administered. Twenty-four hours after stroke induction, plasma MPO-DNA complexes (**E**) were assessed as well as brain infarct volume (**F** and **G**). _n =_ 7–9 per group. (**H**–**K**) Twenty-four hours before stroke induction, neutrophils were depleted by i.p. injection of neutrophil-depleting antibodies. Control mice were injected with an IgG control antibody. Twenty-four hours later, plasma HMGB1 (**H**) and MPO-DNA complexes (**I**) were assessed as well as brain infarct volume (**J** and **K**). _n =_ 7–8 per group. (**L**–**N**) Twenty-four hours before stroke induction, neutrophils were depleted by i.p. injection of neutrophil-depleting antibodies. One hour after stroke onset, either rHMGB1 or vehicle was administered. Twenty-four hours after stroke induction, plasma MPO-DNA complexes (**L**) were assessed as well as brain infarct volume (**M** and **N**). _n =_ 6–7 per group. Groups were compared by ordinary 1-way ANOVA (**A**, **B**, and **D**) or unpaired _t_ test. *_P <_ 0.05, **_P <_ 0.01, ***_P <_ 0.001.

Besides platelets, neutrophils also express and release HMGB1 ([21](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#B21)). To investigate the contribution of neutrophils to the rise of HMGB1 after stroke, we specifically depleted neutrophils before stroke induction ([Supplemental Figure 10](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#sd), A and B, and ref. [22](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#B22)). Twenty-four hours after stroke, neutrophil-depleted mice had similar plasma HMGB1 levels compared with neutrophil-sufficient mice (9.8 ± 3.7 ng/mL vs. 8.8 ± 2.8 ng/mL, respectively; [Figure 5H](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F5)), indicating that neutrophils do not contribute to the rise of plasma HMGB1 after stroke. Nevertheless, neutrophil-depleted mice had reduced levels of circulating MPO-DNA complexes (112.8% ± 46.6% vs. 231.3% ± 74.8%; [Figure 5I](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F5)) and were protected from ischemic stroke brain injury (47.5 ± 15.8 mm 3 vs. 73 ± 19.5 mm 3; [Figure 5, J and K](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F5), and [Supplemental Figure 10](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#sd), C and D). In agreement with our hypothesis, rHMGB1 did not increase plasma NET levels in neutropenic mice (104.7% ± 13.7% vs. 94.7% ± 17.1%; [Figure 5L](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F5)), nor did it alter ischemic stroke brain injury (43.8 ± 19 mm 3 vs. 47.7 ± 12.5 mm 3; [Figure 5, M and N](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F5), and [Supplemental Figure 11](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#sd)).

Finally, we treated WT mice with BoxA ([20](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#B20)), a specific competitive inhibitor of HMGB1, and measured plasma NET levels and stroke outcomes 24 hours after stroke onset. Treatment with BoxA significantly reduced plasma MPO-DNA complexes (144.8% ± 56.2% vs. 275.4% ± 52.5%; [Supplemental Figure 12A](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#sd)) and improved ischemic stroke outcomes (53.9 ± 26.7 mm 3 vs. 88.2 ± 35.2 mm 3; [Supplemental Figure 12](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#sd), B–D), confirming a key role for HMGB1 mediating detrimental NET formation in ischemic stroke.

Platelet-specific HMGB1 knockout reduces platelet-induced NET formation and improves stroke outcomes. To further establish platelet HMGB1 as a critical mediator of NET formation, we isolated platelets and neutrophils from healthy donors and performed in vitro NET assays. Platelets were activated with convulxin (a glycoprotein VI agonist) for 15 minutes and subsequently incubated with neutrophils for 150 minutes, after which NET formation was analyzed by MPO-DNA ELISA. In line with our hypothesis and published literature ([20](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#B20)), the competitive HMGB1 inhibitor, BoxA, significantly reduced platelet-induced NET formation ([Figure 6, A and B](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F6)). Since, in this experimental setup, HMGB1 could be released from neutrophils, we performed a similar experiment in mice, using platelets from platelet-specific HMGB1-knockout mice (HMGB1 fl/fl PF4-cre; KO) or their littermate controls (HMGB1 fl/fl; WT) ([19](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#B19)). Critically, activated HMGB1-KO platelets failed to induce NETs, resulting in significantly reduced MPO-DNA complexes in comparison with WT littermate controls ([Figure 6, C and D](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F6)).

Platelets were activated for 15 minutes with convulxin and then incubated for 2.5 hours with neutrophils in the presence of BoxA or vehicle, after which NETs were quantified using a MPO-DNA ELISA. _n =_ 4 per group. (**C** and **D**) Platelets were isolated from 3 HMGB1 fl/fl (WT) or HMGB1 fl/fl PF4-cre (KO) mice, activated with convulxin, and incubated for 2.5 hours with WT neutrophils, after which NETs were quantified using an MPO-DNA ELISA. _n =_ 3 per group. (**E**–**J**) HMGB1 fl/fl (WT; _n =_ 9) or HMGB1 fl/fl PF4-cre (KO; _n_ = 11) mice were subjected to 1 hour of tMCAO followed by 23 hours of reperfusion. Plasma was isolated and brains were analyzed for ischemic stroke brain damage by TTC staining 24 hours after stroke onset. Upon TTC staining, live brain tissue will stain red, while dead brain tissue will remain white (outlined with black dotted line). (**E**) Plasma HMGB1 levels were measured by ELISA. Subsequently, platelet-specific HMGB1-KO mice and their WT littermate controls were subjected to ischemic stroke, after which plasma was collected and stroke outcomes were analyzed. Twenty-four hours after stroke, HMGB1-KO mice had significantly lower plasma HMGB1 levels compared with WT mice (6.9 ± 3.1 ng/mL vs. 12.7 ± 3.6 ng/mL, respectively; [Figure 6E](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F6)). Importantly, this reduction in plasma HMGB1 was associated with reduced plasma NET levels (141.5% ± 38.1% vs. 233.7% ± 55.5%; [Figure 6F](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F6)) and greatly improved ischemic stroke outcomes ([Figure 6, G–J](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F6)). Together our results confirm a critical role for platelet-derived HMGB1 in the formation of detrimental NETs in the acute phase of ischemic stroke.

Prophylactic treatment with a NET-inhibitory peptide improves stroke outcomes. HMGB1 has been shown to be important in the resolution of inflammation ([23](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#B23)). This limits the clinical use of strategies targeting HMGB1 in ischemic stroke and emphasizes the importance of targeting detrimental downstream effects of HMGB1 signaling. Recently, our laboratory discovered a class of endogenous NET-inhibitory peptides circulating in human umbilical cord blood ([24](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#B24)–[26](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#B26)). Importantly, NET-inhibitory peptides block NET formation without affecting other neutrophil functions, providing an alternative approach to safely target NET formation and immunothrombosis ([25](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#B25), [26](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#B26)). Based on the sequence of the endogenous NET-inhibitory peptide toward the N-terminus of α 1-antitrypsin, we synthethized neonatal NET-inhibitory factor (nNIF) ([26](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#B26)) and assessed its ability to block platelet-induced NET formation in vitro as well as its therapeutic potential in our ischemic stroke model. In both human and mouse neutrophils, nNIF treatment was effective at preventing platelet-induced NET formation ([Supplemental Figure 13](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#sd)). Importantly, when mice were prophylactically treated with nNIF, brain infarct size was reduced significantly in comparison with mice treated with scrambled peptide control (SCR) (37.5 ± 14.6 mm 3 vs. 80.6 ± 23.5 mm 3; [Figure 7, A and B](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F7)). Moreover, this protective effect was also evident by significantly improved neurological and motor function 24 hours after stroke onset ([Figure 7, C and D](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F7)). In accordance with the STAIR criteria ([27](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#B27)), we used male and female mice in our studies and observed an equal protective effect in both sexes ([Figure 7, A–D](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F7)). In a separate experiment, we pretreated mice with nNIF or SCR and followed mice for 7 days after stroke onset. Treatment with nNIF significantly protected mice from stroke-induced mortality ([Figure 7E](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F7)), suggesting that nNIF improves short- and long-term outcomes following ischemic stroke.

nNIF prevents neuronal apoptosis by blocking NET formation. To assess whether nNIF was specifically blocking NET formation, we analyzed brain sections for the presence of NETs by staining for DNA, MPO, and H3cit. nNIF treatment significantly reduced NETs found in ischemic brain tissue after stroke in comparison with SCR-treated animals (11.7% ± 2.7% H3cit+ neutrophils vs. 29.9% ± 6.5% H3cit+ neutrophils; [Figure 7, F–H](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F7)). Moreover, circulating MPO-DNA complexes were significantly reduced in nNIF-treated mice (141.3% ± 43.7% vs. 208.6% ± 31.3%; [Figure 7I](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F7)). As expected, nNIF treatment did not impact HMGB1 levels after stroke ([Supplemental Figure 14](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#sd)). To determine whether reduced NET formation had a functional effect on neuronal cells, we examined neuronal apoptosis after stroke by performing TUNEL staining. In agreement with reduced cerebral infarct sizes, nNIF reduced apoptosis in the ipsilateral brain hemisphere ([Figure 7, J–L](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F7)). Interestingly, nNIF reduced apoptosis in both the infarct core (striatum; 174.8 ± 46.1 cells vs. 320 ± 55.5 cells) and the penumbral cortex (103.2 ± 32.9 cells vs. 198 ± 62.8 cells). Additional staining using NeuN (a neuronal marker; [Supplemental Figure 15](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#sd)) confirmed that apoptotic cells in the brain after stroke were of neuronal origin. Next, we quantified brain neutrophil recruitment by flow cytometry of single-cell suspensions of the ipsilesional brain hemisphere. Specific quantification of neutrophil recruitment revealed no difference between nNIF- and SCR-treated animals (5918 ± 2930 Ly6G+ neutrophils vs. 5006 ± 1743 Ly6G+ neutrophils; [Figure 7, M–O](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F7)). These results were confirmed via immunohistological staining for Ly6G+ neutrophils ([Figure 7P](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F7)).

To confirm a critical role for NETs in mediating ischemic stroke brain injury, we investigated alternative ways of targeting NETs in our ischemic stroke model. PAD4-mediated citrullination of histones is a critical step in the formation of NETs ([28](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#B28)), and this process can be inhibited in vivo by GSK-199, a specific PAD4 inhibitor ([29](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#B29), [30](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#B30)). In agreement with the nNIF results, pretreatment of mice with GSK-199 reduced plasma NET levels (147.5% ± 119.5% vs. 330.4% ± 130.3%; [Figure 8A](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F8)) and improved ischemic stroke outcomes as measured by brain infarct size (44.1 ± 19.8 mm 3 vs. 76.1 ± 22.9 mm 3; [Figure 8, B and C](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F8)) as well as neurological and motor function ([Figure 8, D and E](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F8)). Similar results were obtained when NETs were degraded with DNase I. DNase I reduced NET levels (148.4% ± 82.5% vs. 330.4% ± 130.3%; [Figure 8A](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F8)) and ischemic brain injury (45.7 ± 20.2 mm 3 vs. 76.1 ± 22.9 mm 3; [Figure 8, B and C](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F8)) and improved neurological and motor outcomes ([Figure 8, D and E](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F8)).

(**D**) Bederson’s test was used to assess neurological outcome 24 hours after stroke. (**E**) Twenty-four hours after stroke, motor function was measured using the grip test. Groups were compared by ordinary 1-way ANOVA (**A** and **C**) or Kruskal-Wallis test (**D** and **E**). *_P <_ 0.05, **_P <_ 0.01.

nNIF reduces ischemic stroke brain injury in mice with comorbidities. A common limitation of preclinical stroke studies is the use of young and healthy adult animals. To overcome this limitation, we assessed the effectiveness of nNIF in mice with type 1 diabetes ([Figure 9, A–D](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F9)) and aging (>18 months old; [Figure 9, E–H](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F9)), conditions with an increased stroke risk and aggravated stroke outcomes. Mice were prophylactically treated with nNIF, and 24 hours after stroke, neurological and motor function was assessed before measurement of brain infarction. In diabetic mice, mice treated with nNIF had significantly reduced ischemic stroke brain infarctions (66.6 ± 25.1 mm 3 vs. 107.4 ± 8.9 mm 3; [Figure 9, A and B](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F9)). This translated to significantly improved neurological behavior ([Figure 9C](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F9)) and a trend toward improved motor function ([Figure 9D](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F9)). In 18-month-old mice, nNIF significantly reduced brain damage after stroke as measured by infarct volume (25 ± 6.8 mm 3 vs. 45.9 ± 14.3 mm 3; [Figure 9, E and F](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F9)) and improved neurological function ([Figure 9G](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F9)) and grip strength ([Figure 9H](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F9)).

Therapeutic time window of nNIF in murine ischemic stroke. Next, the therapeutic time window of nNIF in murine ischemic stroke was investigated. For these experiments, nNIF treatment was delayed until 1 or 2 hours after stroke onset, and stroke outcomes were compared with those in SCR-treated mice ([Figure 10A](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F10)). A significant reduction in ischemic stroke brain damage was still observed when nNIF was given 1 hour after stroke onset (46.1 ± 10.5 mm 3 vs. 70.9 ± 14.6 mm 3; [Figure 10, B and C](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F10)). However, protection was lost when nNIF was administered 2 hours after stroke onset (74.3 ± 17.4 mm 3 vs. 70.2 ± 18.2 mm 3; [Figure 10, B and C](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F10)). Notably, while nNIF treatment 1 hour after stroke had only a minor effect on neurological function ([Figure 10D](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F10)), we did observe a significant improvement in motor function ([Figure 10E](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F10)). Importantly, a similar observation was made in diabetic mice. Treatment with nNIF 1 hour after stroke onset in diabetic mice significantly reduced ischemic brain damage (71.4 ± 21.1 mm 3 vs. 101.3 ± 27.2 mm 3; [Figure 10, F and G](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F10)), improved neurological outcomes ([Figure 10H](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F10)), and improved grip strength ([Figure 10I](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F10)).

Acute NET inhibition confers long-term protection from ischemic stroke. Finally, to examine long-term effects of nNIF on stroke outcomes, we subjected mice to 45 minutes of ischemia after which reperfusion was allowed and mice were followed for 3 weeks ([Figure 11A](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F11)). This shorter duration of ischemia was chosen to increase survival rates and have more power to detect potential differences in long-term stroke outcomes. Mice were treated either prophylactically (1 hour before stroke onset) or therapeutically (1 hour after stroke onset) with nNIF or SCR. To monitor overall well-being of mice, weights were measured on a daily basis for the first week after stroke, after which weight was measured every week ([Figure 11B](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F11)). On day 1 after stroke, no differences in weight loss were observed between any of the treatment groups. However, starting from day 2, a clear difference in weight loss became apparent between the nNIF-treated animals and the SCR-treated animals. By 2 weeks after stroke, most mice had recovered to their baseline weight. Also with regard to survival, better outcomes were observed in nNIF-treated animals ([Figure 11C](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F11)). While 28.6% of SCR-treated animals died, only 7.3% of the mice treated with prophylactic nNIF and 9.1% of those treated with therapeutic nNIF succumbed to stroke. However, this difference was not found to be statistically significant (_P =_ 0.17).

(**B**) Weight was measured every day the first week and then every week. (**C**) Survival was monitored daily for 21 days. (**D**) Modified neurological severity scoring (mNSS) was performed every week after stroke for 3 weeks. Groups were compared by 2-way ANOVA (**B**), log-rank test (**C**), or Kruskal-Wallis test (**D** and **E**). *_P <_ 0.05, **_P <_ 0.01, ***_P <_ 0.001.

To assess behavioral and motor stroke outcomes, we performed a modified neurological severity scoring (mNSS) test ([31](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#B31)) and assessed motor function using a rotarod ([32](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#B32)) every week for 3 weeks after stroke onset. The mNSS scores neurological functioning by analyzing a composite of motor, sensory, reflex, and balancing behavior. At all time points assessed, mice treated with prophylactic or therapeutic nNIF had significantly lower mNSS compared with SCR-treated animals ([Figure 11D](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F11)). In parallel, motor coordination was investigated using the rotarod test. In this test, mice are placed on an accelerating rotarod and the time a mouse remains on the device is recorded. Both prophylactic nNIF– and therapeutic nNIF–treated mice performed significantly better compared with SCR-treated animals ([Figure 11E](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225#F11)).

In agreement with a previous report (17), neutrophils were readily found in ipsilesional brain tissue from all stroke patients (Figure 1 and Supplemental Figure 1; supplemental material available online with this article; https://doi.org/10.1172/JCI154225DS1), while neutrophils were mostly absent in contralateral brain tissue from stroke patients (Supplemental Figure 2). Several neutrophils (NE and MPO double-positive cells) in the ipsilesional brain tissue stained positive for H3cit, indicating they either were in the process of NET formation or had already formed a NET (Figure 1 and Supplemental Figure 1). In all patients, both extracellular NETs (arrows) and neutrophils undergoing NET formation (arrowheads) were found (Figure 1, A–D, Supplemental Figure 1, and Supplemental Video 1). In all cases, NE, MPO, DNA, and citrullinated histones colocalized with each other (Figure 1 and Supplemental Figure 1). Neutrophils in the contralesional hemisphere did not stain for H3cit (Supplemental Figure 2).

Markers of immunothrombosis were significantly elevated and plasma DNase activity was greatly reduced in ischemic stroke patients compared with healthy donors (Figure 2). We next used a Spearman correlation analysis to investigate whether markers of immunothrombosis correlated with either stroke severity at admission or stroke outcomes at discharge (Supplemental Table 2). Stroke severity at admission did not correlate with immunothrombosis biomarkers. Interestingly, only markers of NET formation correlated with ischemic stroke outcomes (modified Rankin scale at discharge). Both plasma H3cit and MPO-DNA levels positively correlated with stroke outcomes (r = 0.45, P = 0.024, and r = 0.507, P = 0.01, respectively). Sex, comorbidities, thrombolysis, use of antiplatelet drugs or anticoagulation drugs, or ischemic stroke etiology had no effect on plasma NET levels in our cohort (Supplemental Figure 5).

Platelet-neutrophil interactions mediate NET formation through HMGB1. Platelets are known for their role in NET formation (6), and we observed NETs predominantly in platelet-rich areas of ischemic stroke thrombi as well as in microthrombi in the brain (Figure 1E and Supplemental Figure 3). Additionally, plasma levels of PF4 correlated with both plasma H3cit and MPO-DNA levels in our cohort (r = 0.376, P = 0.024, and r = 0.556, P = 0.001, respectively), implying a role for platelet activation in stroke-induced NET formation. Consistent with previous studies (18), circulating platelet-neutrophil aggregates were significantly increased in stroke patients (Figure 3A and Supplemental Figure 6). Platelets from stroke patients had significantly elevated HMGB1 surface expression (Figure 3, B and C) and increased plasma HMGB1 levels (Figure 3D) compared with healthy donors. Furthermore, HMGB1 predominantly localized at the interface of platelets interacting with neutrophils in ischemic stroke thrombi (Figure 3E). We next examined whether plasma HMGB1 correlated with plasma NET markers and observed that HMGB1 significantly correlated with H3cit and MPO-DNA (r = 0.433, P = 0.0019, and r = 0.3889, P = 0.0057, respectively).

Since, in this experimental setup, HMGB1 could be released from neutrophils, we performed a similar experiment in mice, using platelets from platelet-specific HMGB1-knockout mice (HMGB1 fl/fl PF4-cre; KO) or their littermate controls (HMGB1 fl/fl; WT) (19). This limits the clinical use of strategies targeting HMGB1 in ischemic stroke and emphasizes the importance of targeting detrimental downstream effects of HMGB1 signaling. Importantly, NET-inhibitory peptides block NET formation without affecting other neutrophil functions, providing an alternative approach to safely target NET formation and immunothrombosis (25, 26). In accordance with the STAIR criteria (27), we used male and female mice in our studies and observed an equal protective effect in both sexes (Figure 7, A–D). In a separate experiment, we pretreated mice with nNIF or SCR and followed mice for 7 days after stroke onset. Treatment with nNIF significantly protected mice from stroke-induced mortality (Figure 7E), suggesting that nNIF improves short- and long-term outcomes following ischemic stroke.",
  "summary": "The webpage content focuses on the role of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) in ischemic stroke brain injury. Harmful neutrophil subsets identified are neutrophils undergoing NET formation (H3cit+), which are present in ipsilesional brain tissue from stroke patients and in microthrombi. NET markers (H3cit, MPO-DNA) correlate with worse stroke outcomes. Platelet-neutrophil interactions drive NET formation via platelet-derived HMGB1, as shown by increased HMGB1 in stroke patients, colocalization in thrombi, and correlation with NET markers. Genetic deletion of platelet HMGB1 reduces NET formation and improves stroke outcomes in mice. Targeting NETs directly with a NET-inhibitory peptide (nNIF) reduces infarct volume, neuronal apoptosis, and improves neurological and motor function, even in diabetic and aged mice. The therapeutic window is narrow (effective up to 1 hour post-stroke). The content does not address circadian control of neutrophils, and vascular remodeling is only indirectly referenced through microthrombus formation. Overall, the study establishes NETs as a key mediator of brain injury in ischemic stroke, with platelet HMGB1 as a critical upstream signal."
